article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Sativa
Genetics: South African Sativa × North American hybrid
Breeder: Almighty Seeds
THC Content: 24-27%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: caryophyllene , limonene , pinene
Primary Flavors: Spice, citrus, pine, earth, musk, skunk
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: Mid-to-late September
Indoor Yield: Medium
Outdoor Yield: Variable
Grow Difficulty: Moderate

Lionheart comes from a very different chapter of cannabis breeding than today’s carefully branded Cookies and dessert hybrids . Created by Canada’s Almighty Seeds, this mostly sativa marijuana cultivar emerged from an unexpected combination of African and North American genetics and apparently impressed its breeder enough to become a cornerstone of the company’s small catalog. Period material describes a plant that simply outperformed neighboring selections, developing vigorous branches, sticky resinous flowers and a psychoactive effect remarkable not only for intensity but for how long it continued building. The Big Book of Buds, Volume 2 , published while Almighty Seeds was still active, lists the lineage as African sativa × U.S. #14 sativa and characterizes the high as long-lasting and upbeat.

That history matters because authentic Lionheart has become difficult to find. Almighty Seeds disappeared from the active seed market years ago, and later growers have repeatedly discussed the challenge of locating unquestionable original stock. The name has also been reused for unrelated cannabis, creating an additional layer of confusion. The classic Lionheart covered here is specifically the Almighty Seeds cultivar: an outdoor-oriented sativa with rapid root development, extensive branching, highly resinous but not rock-hard buds and an unusually spicy aroma. Its reputation rests less on modern laboratory numbers than on a distinctive combination of vigorous plant structure and an intense, cumulative cerebral experience.
Genetics and Lineage

The safest way to describe Lionheart’s pedigree is to preserve the uncertainty present in the historical record. The Big Book of Buds identifies the cross as African sativa × U.S. #14 sativa and states that the variety began as a surprise pairing between African and U.S. genetics. The breeder apparently discovered that the resulting plant surpassed other developing lines in both potency and duration of effect. A separate archived Almighty Seeds description is slightly less specific, calling the genetics “probably” South African sativa crossed with a North American hybrid. That qualifier suggests even the breeder did not possess a perfectly documented pedigree for the accidental original cross.

Later cannabis references often simplify U.S. #14 into a named second parent and present Lionheart as a pure sativa. That version is plausible and consistent with period literature, but presenting it as indisputable breeder documentation would go too far. What is much clearer is the plant’s genetic direction. Lionheart behaves like an old-school sativa: long branching, vigorous root growth, relatively airy but heavy flowers, an energetic cerebral effect and an outdoor harvest much earlier than one might expect from tropical genetics.

The African side appears to supply much of that sativa expression, while the unidentified or loosely documented North American contribution seems to have shortened finishing time enough for cultivation in Canada. That combination was particularly valuable in the era when Lionheart was developed. Many tropical sativas could not reliably mature before cold autumn weather arrived in northern latitudes. Lionheart reportedly finished around mid-to-late September while retaining the expansive branching and intense psychoactivity expected from a sativa, making the cross useful not only as a finished weed strain but also as breeding material. Almighty Seeds later used Lionheart in varieties including B-52 Bomber, Cherry Bomb, Desiak, Mountain Lion and Purple Heart.
Effects and Experience

Lionheart’s effect was the feature Almighty Seeds emphasized most strongly. Rather than reaching a quick peak and leveling off, the high was described as increasing with each inhalation. That cumulative character gives the cultivar a different rhythm from marijuana that hits immediately and then settles into a predictable plateau. The first few moments may feel bright and mentally stimulating, but additional consumption can steadily intensify the experience until the cerebral effect becomes considerably more powerful than expected.

At moderate levels, the character is upbeat, active and distinctly sativa-like. Mental energy can increase, conversation becomes engaging and ordinary surroundings may take on greater intensity. Creative thinking and an elevated sense of confidence can accompany the experience, while physical heaviness remains relatively limited compared with indica-dominant weed. The historical breeder description portrayed Lionheart as a true sativa high and specifically emphasized its exceptional strength and duration. The Big Book of Buds similarly describes the effect as long-lasting and upbeat, reinforcing that energetic profile.

The same qualities can become challenging at a high dose. Strong sativa cannabis can produce racing thoughts, restlessness, rapid heart rate or anxiety in sensitive consumers, and Lionheart’s reputation suggests that inexperienced users should not assume its airy flower structure indicates mild potency. Unlike sleepy weed that signals excessive consumption through immediate heaviness, the escalating cerebral character can continue intensifying after several inhalations. Historical material even joked that many people would put a joint down after only a few pulls. While that is colorful breeder language rather than a scientific potency measure, it accurately captures the strain’s old reputation: Lionheart was bred for intensity, not casual mildness.
Medical Benefits

Lionheart’s bright, stimulating character may explain why some medical marijuana consumers historically favored similar sativa-dominant cultivars during daytime hours. Cannabis that produces limited initial sedation may feel more practical to patients who want to remain mentally engaged, while mood elevation and distraction from discomfort can make THC-dominant products appealing to some individuals. Appetite changes and altered pain perception are also well-established effects of cannabinoids, although the response varies substantially between people.

There is no clinical evidence showing that Lionheart itself treats depression, fatigue, pain, anxiety or another medical condition. Named weed strains are not standardized medicines, and authentic original Lionheart is now rare enough that modern products carrying the name may not even represent identical genetics. Broader cannabis research provides some evidence of modest benefits for certain chronic-pain conditions and multiple-sclerosis symptoms, but the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes that evidence for many other proposed uses remains limited or still developing.

The strain’s stimulating reputation also deserves particular caution in medical contexts. A powerful cerebral THC experience may feel uplifting to one patient but intensify anxiety, agitation or insomnia in another. The FDA has not approved cannabis itself as a treatment for any disease or condition, though several cannabinoid-derived or cannabinoid-related prescription medicines have been approved for specific indications. Anyone using marijuana medically should therefore evaluate the tested cannabinoid content of the actual product rather than relying on Lionheart’s historical reputation alone.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Spice sits at the center of Lionheart’s old breeder description. Mature flowers were characterized by a strong, distinctive spicy smell and an extraordinarily sticky texture, with resin production substantial enough that dried buds could break apart almost like soft hash. That combination separates the strain from fruit-forward modern sativas. The aromatic character is closer to pepper, herbs, musk and plant resin, with brighter citrus and pine accents emerging around the edges.

A later Jetty Extracts Lionheart product provides an interesting modern reference point. Jetty described the genetics as African sativa × U.S. #14 and highlighted a terpene-driven profile that blended earthy and musky qualities with citrus, pine and spice. While an extract cannot establish the chemistry of every historical Lionheart plant, the description closely matches earlier accounts of the strain’s pungent, spicy personality.

No trustworthy original terpene laboratory panel survives from Almighty Seeds, so assigning exact dominant terpenes would be speculative. Caryophyllene would be consistent with the pepper-and-spice character, pinene with the evergreen notes and limonene with its citrus edge, but aroma alone cannot prove concentration or rank. Dried Lionheart was also reported to age unusually well. Period documentation describes cured buds turning reddish brown while maintaining quality for an exceptionally long period, an interesting trait in an era when long-term cannabis storage was often less controlled than it is today.
Growing Information

Lionheart was developed with outdoor cultivation firmly in mind. Historical descriptions portray it as a natural multi-branching plant particularly well suited to pots or large containers and capable of thriving even in northern regions such as Canada. Rather than concentrating production into a single central cola, the plant sends long branches outward in multiple directions. Each substantial branch can behave almost like a separate small plant, developing productive flowering sites along much of its length.

The roots are similarly aggressive. Period grow notes emphasize extremely rapid root development, which helps explain the vigor seen above ground. Interestingly, that strength does not necessarily translate into effortless cloning. Lionheart cuttings were historically considered more difficult to root than the established plants themselves were to grow. Once established, however, the cultivar was described as demanding little beyond ordinary care and vigorous enough to compete effectively with surrounding vegetation outdoors.

Flower structure differs from the dense golf-ball buds of modern indica hybrids. Lionheart forms numerous flowers that are heavy and highly resinous without becoming exceptionally hard or compact. That looser construction offers a practical advantage outdoors because the flowers were historically regarded as relatively resistant to mold. As autumn progresses, large fan leaves may yellow naturally and expose more of the interior canopy to sunlight, reducing the amount of leaf material that must later be removed during trimming.

The branching habit creates opportunities for substantial production, but breeder-era references do not provide a reliable standardized yield in grams. Almighty Seeds described the crop as medium yielding, while The Big Book of Buds emphasizes that results vary and depend heavily on plant management and available space. For an old outdoor sativa, that is more informative than a modern-looking grams-per-square-meter estimate invented after the fact. Production comes from the number of productive branches rather than extreme density at any one flowering site.

Archived Almighty Seeds information lists approximately eight weeks of flowering and an outdoor harvest near the end of September, while The Big Book of Buds gives a mid-to-late September harvest. That relatively early finish is one of Lionheart’s most important horticultural characteristics. It allowed a strongly sativa plant to mature in Canadian conditions without requiring the exceptionally long autumn associated with many equatorial varieties. Overall difficulty is moderate: mature plants appear robust and forgiving, but rapid growth, extensive branching and comparatively stubborn cloning make the cultivar less straightforward than a compact indoor hybrid.
FAQ
Is Lionheart indica or sativa?

The original Almighty Seeds Lionheart is a strongly sativa-oriented cultivar. Historical references describe it as an African and American sativa cross, and its long branches, vigorous growth, energetic effects and outdoor-focused cultivation all support that classification.
What are the genetics of Lionheart?

The Big Book of Buds, Volume 2 lists Lionheart as African Sativa × U.S. #14 Sativa. Surviving Almighty Seeds catalog text is slightly less specific, describing the genetics as probably South African Sativa × a North American hybrid. Because the original cross appears to have occurred unexpectedly, the exact second-parent identity should be treated with some historical uncertainty.
Who bred the Lionheart strain?

Almighty Seeds, a Canadian breeder that operated during the earlier modern seed-bank era, created the classic Lionheart covered here. The cultivar subsequently appeared in several Almighty crosses and became one of the breeder’s best remembered sativa lines.
What does Lionheart weed taste like?

Its traditional profile is strongly spicy with earthy, musky and skunky undertones accompanied by pine and citrus. The flowers are also notable for exceptionally sticky resin production rather than the sugary dessert aromas associated with many newer cannabis strains.
How long does Lionheart take to flower?

Archived Almighty Seeds material lists approximately eight weeks of flowering and an outdoor harvest by the end of September. Period documentation in The Big Book of Buds places outdoor maturity around mid-to-late September, making Lionheart unusually early for such a strongly sativa cultivar.
Final Thoughts on Lionheart

Lionheart is valuable partly because it represents a cannabis breeding direction that has become increasingly difficult to find. Its pedigree predates the Cookies , Gelato , Runtz and modern Kush families that now dominate commercial weed menus. Almighty Seeds instead worked with African and North American sativa genetics, accidentally finding a combination vigorous enough for Canadian outdoor cultivation while preserving an unusually intense cerebral effect.

The plant itself is just as unconventional. Rapid roots feed a sprawling network of productive branches; flowers remain somewhat loose yet heavy and resinous; autumn foliage naturally opens the canopy as harvest approaches; and the variety can finish before October despite its strongly sativa nature. Its modest-to-variable yield was apparently considered a reasonable compromise for potency and effect duration, two traits the breeder regarded as exceptional.

Authenticity is now the major complication. Almighty Seeds is no longer an active mainstream breeder, original Lionheart seed stock has become scarce, and unrelated cannabis has occasionally circulated under the same name. That makes historical documentation more useful than modern strain-directory percentages. The original Lionheart is best remembered not as a 26% THC strain or a precise terpene formula, but as Almighty Seeds’ resin-heavy African-American sativa: intensely spicy, highly vigorous, early outdoors and capable of producing a cerebral high whose defining characteristic was that it seemed to keep building long after many other strains would have reached their peak.
